![Image from [Thinking Machines Lab](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/the-future-worth-building-is-human/).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[Thinking Machines Lab](https://thinkingmachines.ai) published [its manifesto](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/the-future-worth-building-is-human/): a case that AI should extend human will and judgment rather than race ahead on its own. The route it lays out is customizable models people can train on their own knowledge, live multimodal interaction, and alignment distributed across many owners instead of decided in a few labs.

The essay builds its case in four moves:

- **The mission and the four bets.** The lab frames its purpose as building AI that "extends human will and judgment," against a default where models are "trained in a handful of places and then frozen," unshaped by the people they serve. It names four technical directions:
  - Train frontier models that advance multimodal interaction and customizability.
  - Build tools that let people make models their own, including "the ability to train model weights."
  - Develop interfaces that widen the human–machine communication channel.
  - Publish research so the power to shape AI is broadly understood.

- **Bringing intelligence to knowledge.** Productive know-how is tacit, local, and continuously updated (a chef refining a recipe, a shopkeeper rearranging a display), so it cannot be written into a database or captured by a model trained once and frozen, citing [Michael Polanyi's *The Tacit Dimension*](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/T/bo6035368.html) and [Friedrich Hayek's *The Use of Knowledge in Society*](https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/hykKnw.html) on why central planning fails. Autonomous AI suffices only where the goal is static and expressible and no hidden knowledge exists, as in chess and math. Elsewhere AI must itself be distributed. The essay invokes Toyota's 2014 decision to [bring master craftsmen back onto the line](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2014-04-06/humans-replacing-robots-herald-toyota-s-vision-of-future) (Mitsuru Kawai: *"to be the master of the machine, you have to have the knowledge and the skills to teach the machine"*) to argue intelligence and knowledge lift each other rather than substitute.

- **Human participation as a technical challenge.** Today's human–AI channel, "a small text box and a long wait," is too narrow and slow for live collaboration, motivating a long-term bet on *interaction models* that handle live, multimodal interaction natively "in the model itself rather than in scaffolding bolted around it." The essay critiques the dominant metric, [METR's time horizon](https://metr.org/time-horizons/) of software tasks models execute autonomously, as measuring only what AI does alone rather than what people and machines accomplish together. It argues its incentives align: a lab selling one model to every customer benefits by absorbing what makes each user distinct, while the lab benefits when customers own and adapt models to their advantages.

- **Decentralized alignment.** Values, like knowledge, resist consolidation, yet AI's values are decided in a handful of places, and "a single locus of value alignment ... becomes a locus of power to be captured." It ties this to the concentration danger in [*The Intelligence Curse*](https://intelligence-curse.ai/) and cites Leo XIV's [*Magnifica Humanitas*](https://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/encyclicals/documents/20260515-magnifica-humanitas.html) ("a more moral AI is not enough if that morality is determined by a few"), noting each lab now trains its next flagship on the previous one's outputs, so everyone inherits one character. Its fix is to encode values in user-owned weights rather than prompts: a prompt-only change leaves deeper habits intact, and a prompt-malleable central model is attack-vulnerable ([Gwern's *Guardian Angels*](https://gwern.net/guardian-angel)). It concedes, via [von Neumann](https://sseh.uchicago.edu/doc/von_Neumann_1955.pdf), that the power to shape a model for good is also the power to shape it for ill, and envisions alignment as an ecosystem of diverse AIs "raised in different places, disagreeing, competing, and learning from each other."

- **The future worth building.** Closing on [Hannah Arendt's *The Human Condition*](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/H/bo29137972.html), the essay rejects framing human involvement as a trade-off against capability or safety, casting participation, ownership, and diverse alignment as technical problems to solve rather than costs to pay: "the future is not a choice between human dominance and rapid obsolescence."

## My Notes

- **The whole case is a bet on tacit knowledge.** Recast as model architecture, Hayek's argument says knowledge is too tacit and local to freeze into one model. The essay's own carve-out marks where that stops: autonomous AI is enough wherever a goal is static, expressible, and hides no knowledge, as in chess and math. The bet is that most valuable work stays outside that zone. As models improve and more goals turn out to be expressible, the zone may keep growing, and where the line settles decides how much of the case survives.

- **Distributing alignment also distributes the risk.** The essay's fix for a single locus of power, encoding values in user-owned weights rather than prompts, spreads the risk of misuse as widely as the power itself. It concedes a prompt-malleable central model is attack-vulnerable, but never resolves why widely distributed weights are safer rather than just differently exposed.

- **What keeps the lab competitive if customers own the weights?** The essay argues its incentives are aligned: it benefits when customers own and adapt their own models rather than renting one. That is a candid business case, but it leaves a question unanswered: where the durable advantage comes from once the customer holds the weights.
  - **The moat.** Selling a model and handing over the weights gives away the asset other labs rent out. The four technical directions imply an answer (stay on the frontier, own the tooling and the interaction layer), but the essay does not spell out how those sustain a business when each customer's real value lives in weights the lab no longer controls.
  - **Portability.** Weights are tied to an architecture. When the base model is replaced, especially if the architecture changes, a customer's fine-tuned weights do not obviously transfer, and they may have to retrain each generation. Their data and training recipes survive the switch and can be reapplied to whatever model comes next.
